issues.legal_issue: An administrative commissioner hearing a statutory appeal is not a court where the governing enactment distinguishes that authority from the civil courts it defines as courts.
material_facts: The commissioner was appointed by the government as an authority under the enactment and was empowered to hear the statutory appeal.
The enactment defined a court by reference to specified civil courts and separately identified the commissioner as an authority.
An aggrieved party could challenge the commissioner’s order by bringing a suit in the defined court.
issues.conclusion: The commissioner was not a court within the meaning of the governing enactment.
issues.legal_principle: The enactment’s separate definitions and structure showed that the commissioner was an administrative authority, while “court” meant a civil court constituted to administer justice. In S. Parthy v. State Bank of India, an authority with court-like trappings was treated as a court for the particular purpose of Section 14 of the Limitation Act; that decision did not govern the distinct question of Section 5 here. The Court relied on the three-Judge decision in Commissioner of Sales Tax, U.P. v. Parson Tools and Plants, which held that statutory appellate and revisional authorities were not courts for purposes of the Limitation Act.

predicates.statutory_appeal_proceeding: A party brought an appeal under a special enactment before an authority established or designated by that enactment.
predicates.authority_is_separately_created_from_cou: The enactment identifies the appeal-hearing authority separately from the civil courts that it establishes or recognizes.
predicates.enactment_defines_court_as_civil_court: The enactment uses the term court to refer to civil courts rather than to the statutory appeal-hearing authority.

issues.definition: When a statutory appeal is heard by an authority distinct from the civil courts that the enactment identifies as courts, the appeal-hearing authority is not a court.

issues.legal_issue: The general application of limitation-law provisions through the special-law saving provision does not extend to appeals or applications filed before statutory authorities that are not courts.
material_facts: The special enactment prescribed a period for filing an appeal before the commissioner, a statutory authority rather than a court.
The appellant argued that the general saving provision in the Limitation Act could not make Section 5 applicable to an appeal before that authority.
The Court considered authorities addressing whether the Limitation Act applies to proceedings before courts or non-court tribunals.
issues.conclusion: The special-law saving provision did not apply to the statutory appeal before the commissioner, and could not make Section 5 applicable to it.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that suits, appeals and applications referred to in the Limitation Act and its Schedule are proceedings to be filed in court. Section 29(2) therefore applies where a special or local law prescribes a different limitation period for a suit, appeal or application in court, not one before a statutory authority or tribunal. The Court relied on Nityananda M. Joshi v. Life Insurance Corporation of India, Town Municipal Council, Athani v. Presiding Officer, Labour Court, Sakuru v. Tanaji, Officer on Special Duty (Land Acquisition) v. Shah Manilal Chandulal, Consolidated Engineering Enterprises v. Principal Secretary, Irrigation Department, and M.P. Steel Corporation v. Commissioner of Central Excise. It followed Parson Tools and Plants over the contrary treatment of Section 12(2) in Commissioner of Sales Tax, U.P. v. Madan Lal Das & Sons, which had not considered the earlier equal-strength decision. Mukri Gopalan v. Cheppilat Puthanpurayil Aboobacker was treated as no longer good law to the extent it conflicted with the later binding decisions. The Court distinguished State of Madhya Pradesh v. Anshuman Shukla because the revision there was before the High Court, a court.

predicates.special_law_proceeding: A person pursued a suit, appeal, or application created or regulated by a special or local enactment.
predicates.special_law_prescribes_a_limitation_peri: The special or local enactment sets a limitation period for the proceeding.
predicates.filing_forum_is_statutory_authority_not_: The proceeding is filed before a statutory authority or tribunal that is not a court.

issues.definition: The general limitation saving does not apply when a special-law proceeding with its own limitation period is filed before a statutory authority rather than a court.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory commissioner cannot condone a late appeal by applying the general power to extend time in the Limitation Act where that Act does not apply to the proceeding.
material_facts: A respondent filed a statutory appeal before the commissioner after the prescribed filing period had expired.
The respondent sought condonation of a 266-day delay, attributing it to illness that prevented travel to instruct counsel.
The commissioner condoned the delay, and the appellant challenged that order.
The appeal was before a statutory authority that the Court held was not a court.
issues.conclusion: The commissioner was not entitled to condone the delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act; the order condoning delay was set aside and the delayed appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5 allows a court to admit a late appeal or application on sufficient cause, but it does not, by itself, apply to proceedings before non-court statutory authorities. Section 29(2) does not extend Section 5 to such proceedings. The Court relied on Nityananda M. Joshi, Athani, Parson Tools and Plants, Sakuru, Shah Manilal Chandulal, Consolidated Engineering Enterprises and M.P. Steel Corporation, and held that Mukri Gopalan did not govern in light of the later binding decisions.

rule.if: statutory_appeal_proceeding and appeal_is_late and appeal_forum_is_not_a_court and no_special_law_authorizes_extension

predicates.statutory_appeal_proceeding: A party filed an appeal provided by a special or local enactment before the authority designated by that enactment.
predicates.appeal_is_late: The party filed the appeal after the filing period prescribed for it had expired.
predicates.appeal_forum_is_not_a_court: The authority hearing the appeal is not a court.
predicates.no_special_law_authorizes_extension: The governing enactment does not separately authorize the appeal-hearing authority to extend the filing period on sufficient cause.

issues.definition: A late statutory appeal before a non-court authority cannot be admitted under a general sufficient-cause power if the governing enactment does not authorize an extension.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory scheme that provides for civil-procedure-like hearings, excludes only specified time for obtaining a copy, and gives the authority a separate review power does not make the general power to condone delay applicable.
material_facts: The enactment required appeals to be heard, as nearly as may be, according to civil-procedure rules and applied specified evidence and oath rules.
A separate provision excluded the time required to obtain a certified copy when computing limitation.
The enactment empowered the commissioner to examine certain orders on the commissioner’s own initiative when no appeal had been filed in time.
The rules governing applications, appeals and inquiries supplied procedural details but did not provide for condonation under Section 5.
issues.conclusion: The statutory scheme did not make Section 5 of the Limitation Act applicable to appeals before the commissioner.
issues.legal_principle: A special or local enactment may apply or exclude limitation-law provisions through its statutory scheme, but procedural powers resembling those of a court do not alone make the Limitation Act applicable. The Court read the civil-procedure provision as governing procedure only, the certified-copy provision as providing only for computation of time, and the commissioner’s own-initiative power as supporting the conclusion that the legislature did not contemplate condonation under Section 5. It also relied on Section 69(2), Section 110 and Section 115 of the governing enactment, and on the principle in Sakuru that an express or scheme-based statutory authorization is needed to apply Section 5 before a non-court authority.

rule.if: statutory_appeal_proceeding and authority_is_not_a_court and procedure_borrows_court_process and limitation_scheme_only_excludes_copy_time and authority_has_own_initiative_review_power

predicates.statutory_appeal_proceeding: A party pursued an appeal created by a special or local enactment before the authority designated to hear it.
predicates.authority_is_not_a_court: The appeal-hearing authority is a statutory authority rather than a court.
predicates.procedure_borrows_court_process: The enactment directs the authority to follow court-like procedural rules for hearing or inquiry.
predicates.limitation_scheme_only_excludes_copy_tim: The enactment addresses limitation by allowing specified time for obtaining a copy to be excluded, without providing a general power to extend time for sufficient cause.
predicates.authority_has_own_initiative_review_powe: The enactment allows the authority to examine or correct certain orders on its own initiative when no timely appeal is filed.

issues.definition: Where a non-court authority follows court-like procedures but the limitation scheme only provides for excluding copy-obtaining time and gives the authority a separate own-initiative review power, the scheme does not include a general power to condone delay.
